provision: Article V amendment procedure (with the Electoral College as the test case of rigidity)
text_summary: Amendments need two-thirds of both houses of Congress (or a convention called by two-thirds of the states) and ratification by three-quarters of the states. Article V also entrenches equal state representation in the Senate against amendment without a state's consent.
history: About 11,985 amendment measures were introduced in Congress between 1789 and January 2025; Congress approved 33 and the states ratified 27. The convention route has never been used. The last substantive amendment (26th, voting age 18) dates from 1971; the 27th (1992) was a leftover proposed in 1789. The Electoral College shows the cost of rigidity: five presidents took office after losing the popular vote (1824, 1876, 1888, 2000, 2016), the Bayh-Celler abolition amendment cleared the House in 1969 but died in the Senate (not verified in an opened source), and reform has since moved to a workaround, the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, which by September 2026 covered 18 states plus DC with 222 of the 270 electoral votes needed.

assessment.reasoning: The procedure gave the text 235 years of continuity and blocked bad ideas as well as good ones. But a bar this high leaves widely recognised defects (Electoral College, Senate malapportionment) unamendable in practice and pushes change into judicial interpretation and interstate workarounds. Scholars disagree whether that rigidity is a feature (stability) or the main reason the US text now looks archaic; Elkins, Ginsburg and Melton count flexibility as a survival factor, Levinson calls Article V the constitution's central flaw.

lesson: Set the amendment bar high enough to prevent capture but low enough that a broad supermajority can actually fix known defects, and never let a procedural rule make one clause permanently untouchable except for core rights.
